newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM says Hanson support won't last.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM says Hanson support won't last.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard predicted on Wednesday that support for race row politician Pauline Hanson would fall when it became obvious that she could not solve Australia's problems.
"I believe that that support will disappear once people realise that she doesn't have any superior answers," Howard told Melbourne radio station 3AW.

Howard was asked about a Morgan poll, released on Tuesday, which found the independent Queensland MP's newly-formed "One Nation" party would attract 10 percent voter support for the lower house of parliament.
He said the Morgan poll results did not come as a surprise to him at all as Hanson represented the fears, concerns and sense of insecurity that many Australians were feeling.
"We are living at the moment at a time of tremendous change and upheaval and people feel uncertain, they feel insecure, they feel their lives are changing economically and socially," Howard said.

"When somebody comes along, as she has done, and offers simplistic solutions, it's easy to cream six or eight or 10 points in an opinion poll mid-term," he said, adding that he had not heard any serious, long-term answers from her.

Howard said he disagreed with Queensland state Premier Rob Borbidge's claim that the poll results showed support for Hanson's right-wing party could sweep the nation. According to the Morgan poll, it has already become Australia's third political force less than three weeks after its launch.
A separate poll published in the Sydney Morning Herald newspaper on Wednesday said one in four voters would consider voting for the One Nation party in the lower house of parliament.
It found 28 percent of voters would consider voting for the party for the upper house Senate -- where it would be easier for Hanson to gain the balance of power.
Howard warned Borbidge against paying too much attention to poll results.
"I would counsel all of my colleagues ... to remember the transient appeal of the populist who pretends to articulate the concerns but has none of the answers," Howard said.
"They've come and gone in the past and I believe that that will be the case with this particular phenomenon."
Hanson was elected as an independent in what had been viewed as a safe Labor seat after being disowned by Howard's Liberal Party for what was seen as her racist views.

She sparked a national race row last year when she claimed that Australia was at risk of being swamped by Asian immigrants. She has also campaigned against what she describes as excessive government welfare for Aborigines.
